extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (Kantian philosophy, philosophy of religion, epistemology)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and conceptual criteria for assessing proofs and beliefs about supersensible objects (God, immortality, highest good) within Kant's distinction between theoretical and practical reason. Focuses on what kinds of proof/conviction are possible, limits of analogy/hypothesis/probability, and the status of moral faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof should convince, not merely persuade
rubrics_metrics.description: The ground of proof or the conclusion should not persuade but convince (or at least tend to conviction); it must be an objectively valid and logical ground of cognition, not merely a subjective/aesthetical determining ground of assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid proofs that rely on rhetorical eloquence or the subjective propensity of human reason to prefer a single principle; expose such illusions even when they have popular usefulness. Persuasion rooted in subjective aesthetic grounds ensnares the Understanding but does not produce genuine conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish proofs that aim 'in themselves' from those that aim 'for us'
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof can either decide what the object is in itself (κατ’ ἀλήθειαν) — based on adequate principles for the determinant judgement (theoretical) — or what it is for us (κατ’ ἄνθρωπον) — based on principles for the reflective judgement (practical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit which kind of proof is attempted: only the first can aim at theoretical conviction about objects-in-themselves; the second may yield moral conviction adequate for practical purposes but not theoretical knowledge of the supersensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate physical Teleology from moral Teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument must keep distinct the parts belonging to physical teleology (purposes of nature) and moral teleology (practical final purpose), because blending them obscures where the proper force of the proof lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate an explanation of natural purposiveness with the moral argument for God; combine them only to indicate practical reality of an Idea, but treat their evidential roles separately when scrutinising logical strictness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical syllogisms cannot yield cognition of the supersensible
rubrics_metrics.description: No intuition possible for us corresponds to the concept of a Being beyond nature, so logically accurate proofs (deductive syllogisms) cannot produce ampliative theoretical cognition of such a supersensible Being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise the limits of purely deductive argument when the concept lacks any sensible correlate; such proofs cannot increase theoretical knowledge about God or the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy is limited where dissimilarities exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Although we can think one thing by analogy with another, we cannot transfer specific determinations across domains where they are dissimilar; analogical reasoning cannot legitimately ascribe to a supersensible cause the specific properties known only in sensible beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogy only to suggest a mode of conception (e.g., divine causality analogised to human understanding), but avoid inferring particular attributes (e.g., human-like understanding) for the supersensible Being from that analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability has no place for a priori judgements about the supersensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability presupposes a series of grounds that can be completed toward certainty; empirical grounds that lie within experience cannot be combined with a priori claims about what lies outside all possible experience to produce legitimate probability for the supersensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat empirical indicators of purposiveness as providing probabilistic support for transcendent claims; such mixing of kinds of grounds invalidates any claim to probability about God or immortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses require certainty of possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If a hypothesis is offered to explain a phenomenon, at least the possibility of what is posited must be completely certain; one cannot legitimately hypothesise the possibility of a supersensible Being determinate in concept without grounds for that possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adopting hypotheses about supersensible objects whose possibility is themselves doubtful; the mere logical non-contradiction of an idea does not establish the possibility of its object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify claims into things of opinion, fact, or faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognisable things fall into: (1) things of opinion (opinabile) — empirical in kind though perhaps currently unobservable; (2) things of fact (scibile) — whose objective reality can be proved via intuition/experience; (3) things of faith (mere credibile) — transcendent for theoretical use but commanded by pure practical Reason (e.g., highest good, God, immortality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply different standards: do not demand empirical proof for things of faith (they are postulates of practical reason); require empirical/intuition-based proof for scibilia; treat opinabilia as empirically possible but uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral faith (things of faith) are postulates for practical Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects which must be thought a priori for the use of pure practical Reason (as consequences or grounds) but are transcendent for theoretical use (e.g., the highest good, God, immortality) are 'things of faith' and are to be assumed as postulates for moral action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such beliefs are not theoretical knowledge; they are adopted because practical Reason commands their assumption as conditions for the possibility of fulfilling moral ends. Treat them as moral convictions adequate for conduct, not as objects of speculative proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith is a moral habit (habitus), not a theoretical act
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith, absolutely so called, is the moral attitude of Reason to assume as true what is unattainable by theoretical cognition, i.e., a constant principle to assume as true what must be presupposed as condition of the highest moral final purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand faith as a stable practical commitment that sustains moral action; it compensates for the absence of theoretical conviction without amounting to dogmatic knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral proof can establish practical reality without theoretical determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral argument (moral Teleology) establishes the actuality of a highest morally-legislating Author sufficiently for the practical use of Reason, giving practical reality to the Idea of God, but it does not determine anything theoretically about His being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use moral proof to justify postulates necessary for moral deliberation and action; do not mistake this for a theoretical proof that provides knowledge of the supersensible Being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of completing concepts arbitrarily when seeking unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Human reason has a propensity to complete a principle (e.g., many natural marks of intelligence) into one all-sufficient cause (attributing omniscience, omnipotence, moral will), but such completions may be arbitrary and illusory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose the arbitrary supplementation of concepts and distinguish between subjective persuasiveness and objective logical grounds; philosophers should clarify where conviction ends and persuasion begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of natural purposiveness and moral purpose is important for practical reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical purposiveness in nature alone cannot establish the objective reality of the Idea of God as moral Author; when combined with the concept of moral purpose and the maxim seeking unity of principles, these considerations gain importance for the practical reality of the Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing for the practical reality of the Idea of God, show how empirical awareness of purposiveness in nature, together with moral requirements, supports the postulate — but make clear this supplies practical (reflective) justification, not theoretical proof.
